newsitem.title: USA: U.S. helicopters fired on, Albania airlift halted.
newsitem.headline: U.S. helicopters fired on, Albania airlift halted.

text.p: The United States suspended its military evacuation of Americans from Albania on Friday after a shoulder-launched missile and machine gun were fired at two Marine helicopter gunships, U.S. officials said.
Defence Secretary William Cohen told reporters: "According to reports that we received from the pilots, they were fired upon. That fire was returned. They were not struck by any of the fire."
Cohen said the evacuation, which began on Thursday, "is terminated for the next several hours" while commanders on the ground assess whether it can go ahead safely.
The operation began after anarchy spread to Tirana, capital of the impoverished Balkan state, with gunfire in the streets and widespread looting of armouries and food stores.

In the first attack early on Friday, a group of Albanians fired a 14.5 mm anti-aircraft gun at a Marine Cobra, Lt. Gen. Peter Pace, director of operations for the joint chiefs of staff, told reporters. He said the Cobra fired back and the crowd dispersed. Within an hour, another Marine Cobra saw a shoulder missile being launched and also returned fire.

He said Gen. George Joulwan, supreme allied commander of NATO, and Adm. Charles Abbot, commander of the U.S. 6th Fleet, must decide whether to resume the helicopter evacuation, take Americans out by ship or secure the airport at Tirana and fly them out.

Defence officials said 408 Americans were evacuated from Tirana before the suspension and about 150 marines remained in Albania. Evacuees were taken to three helicopter landing ships offshore and then by other helicopters to Brindisi in Italy.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said he believed another 500 to 600 Americans wanted to leave. Washington also intends to keep its Tirana embassy operational, with ambassador Marisa Lino and 17 other staff, he said.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said the evacuees included non-essential embassy employees, their family members and other Americans. She said "the situation in Tirana itself is somewhat chaotic in terms of not having a government that is totally in control."
When asked about reports that Albanaian President Sali Berisha had fled, she said: "Our information is we believe that he is in Tirana ... Ambassador (Marisa) Lino is watching that very carefully."
Burns said the only way to bring order to Albania was for the rebels to lay down their arms and for the political coalition in Tirana to seek out the leaders of the insurgents and talk with them.
"We believe it is incumbent upon President Berisha and the other politicians in Albania to find those people, seek them out, and try to establish a political dialogue," he said.

"There is the possibility of Western economic aid through the World Bank, through the International Monetary Fund, through the United States and other governments. But that kind of assistance cannot arrive in a situation of chaos and disorder and civil war," he said.

Asked whether the United States was considering any military involvement itself to restore order, Cohen said: "What I'm saying is that we're watching it closely. Our sole motivation right now, and goal and objective is to get the Americans out of there safely.
"Beyond that there is no planning for U.S. intervention. We're watching it very closely. We're talking with our allies."
